stem:
An interviewer asks you to implement `ReturnType` without the built-in. Which definition passes all three checks?

```ts
type A = MyReturnType<() => string>;                     // string
type B = MyReturnType<(a: number, b: string) => boolean>; // boolean
type C = MyReturnType<() => Promise<number>>;            // Promise<number>
```

options.text:
```ts
type MyReturnType<T> =
  T extends (...args: any[]) => infer R ? R : never;
```
options.why: `(...args: any[])` accepts a function with any parameter list, and `infer R` captures the return type exactly as declared, so all three checks pass.

options.text:
```ts
type MyReturnType<T> =
  T extends () => infer R ? R : never;
```
options.why: A function with two required parameters is not assignable to `() => R`, so `B` becomes `never`.

options.text:
```ts
type MyReturnType<T> =
  T extends (...args: any[]) => infer R ? Awaited<R> : never;
```
options.why: `Awaited` unwraps the promise, so `C` becomes `number` instead of `Promise<number>`.

options.text:
```ts
type MyReturnType<T> =
  T extends (...args: infer R) => any ? R : never;
```
options.why: `infer` sits in the parameter position, so this returns the parameter tuple: `B` becomes `[a: number, b: string]`.

explanation: `ReturnType` is a one-line conditional type: match `T` against a function type whose parameters accept anything, and put `infer R` where the return type goes. The interviewer is checking three things: that you know where `infer` goes, that the parameter list must accept any arity (`...args: any[]`), and that `ReturnType` reports the return type as declared, without unwrapping promises.

options.text: `A` is `unknown` and `B` is `string[]`
options.why: When `infer` matches a generic signature, TypeScript replaces each type parameter with its constraint: an unconstrained `T` becomes `unknown`, and `T extends string` becomes `string`.

options.text: `A` is `T` and `B` is `T[]`
options.why: A type parameter cannot leak out of the signature that declares it. TypeScript substitutes the constraint instead.

options.text: `A` is `any` and `B` is `any[]`, since generics are erased
options.why: The fallback is the constraint, not `any`. Unconstrained type parameters have the implicit constraint `unknown`.

options.text: `A` is `never` and `B` is `never[]`
options.why: The match succeeds, because a generic function is still a function, so the `never` branch is not used.

explanation: `ReturnType<typeof genericFn>` cannot know which `T` you mean, so it uses each type parameter's constraint. To get a specific result, use an instantiation expression (TypeScript 4.7+): `ReturnType<typeof identity<number>>` is `number`. Interviewers ask this as a follow-up to "implement `ReturnType`" to see whether you understand how `infer` handles generic signatures.

stem: Which three statements about the built-in `ReturnType<T>` are true? (Choose three.)

options.text: `ReturnType<string>` is a compile error, because the type parameter is constrained to `(...args: any) => any`.
options.why: The library declaration is `type ReturnType<T extends (...args: any) => any> = ...`, so non-function arguments fail the constraint.

options.text: For an overloaded function, it reports the return type of the last overload signature.
options.why: Inference from an overloaded type uses the last signature, which is usually the most general one.

options.text: For a union of function types it distributes, so `ReturnType<(() => string) | (() => number)>` is `string | number`.
options.why: `T` is checked as a naked type parameter, so the conditional runs once for each union member and the results are joined.

options.text: `ReturnType<() => Promise<number>>` is `number`, because it unwraps promises.
options.why: It reports `Promise<number>`. Combine it with `Awaited` to unwrap: `Awaited<ReturnType<typeof fn>>`.

options.text: `ReturnType<typeof SomeClass>` gives the instance type of the class.
options.why: A class constructor type has a construct signature, not a call signature, so this fails the constraint. Use `InstanceType<typeof SomeClass>`.

options.text: It works only on functions declared with the `function` keyword, not on arrow functions or methods.
options.why: It works on any type with a call signature, including arrow functions and method types such as `typeof obj.method`.

explanation: The built-in is `type ReturnType<T extends (...args: any) => any> = T extends (...args: any) => infer R ? R : any`. The constraint is what turns misuse into an error, the conditional is distributive over unions, and overloads resolve to the last signature. Interviewers use these edge cases to tell apart someone who memorised the one-liner from someone who understands it.

stem:
Which two `Flatten` implementations pass all of these checks? (Choose two.)

```ts
type A = Flatten<[1, [2, [3]]]>;        // [1, 2, 3]
type B = Flatten<[[1, [2]], 3, [[4]]]>; // [1, 2, 3, 4]
type C = Flatten<[]>;                   // []
```

options.text:
```ts
type Flatten<T extends unknown[]> =
  T extends [infer H, ...infer R]
    ? H extends unknown[] ? [...Flatten<H>, ...Flatten<R>] : [H, ...Flatten<R>]
    : [];
```
options.why: It flattens the head recursively when it is an array, flattens the rest, and spreads both, so every nesting level disappears.

options.text:
```ts
type Flatten<T extends unknown[]> =
  T extends [infer H, ...infer R]
    ? H extends unknown[] ? Flatten<[...H, ...R]> : [H, ...Flatten<R>]
    : [];
```
options.why: It splices a nested head back into the list and processes it again. This also reaches every level and gives the same tuples.

options.text:
```ts
type Flatten<T extends unknown[]> =
  T extends [infer H, ...infer R]
    ? H extends unknown[] ? [...H, ...Flatten<R>] : [H, ...Flatten<R>]
    : [];
```
options.why: It spreads a nested array without flattening it, so only one level is removed: `A` becomes `[1, 2, [3]]`.

options.text:
```ts
type Flatten<T extends unknown[]> =
  T extends [infer H, ...infer R]
    ? H extends unknown[] ? [Flatten<H>, ...Flatten<R>] : [H, ...Flatten<R>]
    : [];
```
options.why: `Flatten<H>` is placed as a single element instead of being spread, so the nesting stays: `A` is `[1, [2, [3]]]`.

options.text:
```ts
type Flatten<T extends unknown[]> =
  T[number] extends infer U ? (U extends unknown[] ? Flatten<U> : U) : never;
```
options.why: Indexing with `[number]` produces a union of elements, so `A` becomes `1 | 2 | 3`. The order and the tuple shape are lost.

explanation: Type-level `Flatten` walks the tuple with `[infer H, ...infer R]`. When the head is itself an array, it must be flattened again, either by recursing on it and spreading the result or by splicing it back into the list. The interviewer is looking for the base case (`[]`), recursion on both parts, and spreading instead of nesting.

stem:
What does `A` resolve to?

```ts
type FlattenOnce<T extends unknown[]> =
  T extends [infer H, ...infer R]
    ? H extends unknown[] ? [...H, ...FlattenOnce<R>] : [H, ...FlattenOnce<R>]
    : [];

type A = FlattenOnce<[1, [2, [3]], 4]>;
```

options.why: The nested `[2, [3]]` is spread one level, so its elements `2` and `[3]` become top-level elements. `[3]` itself is never revisited.
That needs a recursive call on `H` too. Here only the rest `R` is recursed into.
The `H extends unknown[]` branch spreads `H`, so one level of nesting is removed.
Spreading a tuple into a tuple keeps a tuple with fixed positions. It does not widen to an array of a union.

explanation: This mirrors `Array.prototype.flat()` with the default depth of 1. Recursion runs over the rest of the list, but a spread head is not looked at again. For a full flatten you also recurse into `H`. Interviewers often ask for the one-level version first and then for the deep one.

stem: You need to type a `flattenDeep` function so that `flattenDeep([1, [2, [3]]])` has the type `number[]`. Which declaration does that?

options.why: `DeepFlat` keeps unwrapping array element types until it reaches a non-array type, so `(number | (number | number[])[])[]` reduces to `number`.
`T` is inferred as the element type `number | (number | number[])[]`, so the result keeps the nested array types.
The call does not compile: `1` is not an array, so the argument does not match `T[][]`.
It compiles, but the result is `unknown[]`, so callers lose the element type and have to cast.

explanation: A typed `flatten` needs a recursive conditional type that unwraps element types. The standard library does something similar: `Array.prototype.flat` returns `FlatArray<Arr, Depth>[]`, so `[1, [2, [3]]].flat()` is typed `(number | number[])[]`. The interviewer wants to see the value-level function and the type-level recursion line up.

stem: Which `JSONValue` type accepts `{ a: [1, 'x', { b: null }], c: true }` but rejects `{ d: new Date() }`, `{ u: undefined }` and `{ f: () => 1 }` under `strict`?

options.text:
```ts
type JSONValue =
  | string | number | boolean | null
  | JSONValue[]
  | { [key: string]: JSONValue };
```
options.why: Arrays and object values must themselves be `JSONValue`, so nesting works at any depth, while `Date`, `undefined` and functions match no member.
`object` accepts any non-primitive, including `Date` instances and functions.

options.text:
```ts
type JSONValue =
  | string | number | boolean | null
  | any[]
  | Record<string, any>;
```
options.why: `any` inside the array and record lets anything through, including `undefined` and functions.

options.text:
```ts
type JSONValue =
  | string | number | boolean
  | JSONValue[]
  | { [key: string]: JSONValue };
```
options.why: `null` is missing, so the valid JSON `{ b: null }` is rejected under `strictNullChecks`.

explanation: A recursive type alias can refer to itself inside an array or an object type (TypeScript 3.7+). The members are exactly the JSON value kinds: the four primitives including `null`, arrays of JSON values, and string-keyed objects of JSON values. The interviewer is checking that you avoid `any` and `object`, which would make the type useless.

stem: Which three type aliases compile? (Choose three.)

options.why: The self-reference is inside an array type, which TypeScript resolves lazily, so the alias is allowed.
Properties of an object type are resolved lazily, so a tree node can refer to its own type.
Tuple element types are also deferred, so this recursive binary structure compiles.
A bare union member must be resolved immediately, so tsc reports TS2456: the alias circularly references itself.
The check type of a conditional is needed straight away, so this is also a circular reference error.
`keyof` needs the full type of its operand, which is the alias being defined, so this is circular too.

explanation: Recursive type aliases work when the self-reference sits somewhere TypeScript can defer: inside an array, tuple, object property or the type arguments of an interface or class. A reference that must be resolved to produce the alias itself, such as a bare union member, a conditional check type or `keyof`, is a circularity error. Interviewers ask this when you type trees, nested menus or JSON.

options.text: An object literal type written with `type` gets an implicit index signature, so `UserT` fits `{ [key: string]: JSONValue }`. An interface does not, because declaration merging could still add members to it.
options.why: This is the documented difference. Interfaces stay open to augmentation, so TypeScript will not assume all their properties match an index signature.

options.text: Interfaces cannot appear inside recursive types, so `UserI` stops the recursion.
options.why: Interfaces can take part in recursive types. The failure is about index signatures, not recursion.

options.text: Interfaces are compared nominally, so `UserI` matches only types that explicitly `extend` it.
options.why: Interfaces are compared structurally like any other object type.

options.text: `UserI` has a hidden `constructor` property, which is not a valid JSON value.
options.why: Interfaces do not get hidden members. Both declarations describe exactly the same two properties.

explanation: This gotcha shows up as soon as you type JSON payloads. To fix it, use a `type` alias for the payload, or declare `interface UserI extends Record<string, JSONValue> { ... }`. The interviewer is probing whether you know that implicit index signatures are one real behavioural difference between `type` and `interface`.

stem:
Which `Trim` passes all three checks?

```ts
type WS = ' ' | '\n' | '\t';

type A = Trim<'  hi  '>;   // 'hi'
type B = Trim<'hi   '>;    // 'hi'
type C = Trim<'\n hi\t'>; // 'hi'
```

options.text:
```ts
type Trim<S extends string> =
  S extends `${WS}${infer R}` ? Trim<R>
  : S extends `${infer L}${WS}` ? Trim<L>
  : S;
```
options.why: It removes one whitespace character from either end per step and recurses until neither end matches, which handles uneven and mixed whitespace.

options.text:
```ts
type Trim<S extends string> =
  S extends `${WS}${infer R}` ? Trim<R> : S;
```
options.why: This only trims the left side: `A` becomes `'hi  '` and `B` stays `'hi   '`.

options.text:
```ts
type Trim<S extends string> =
  S extends ` ${infer M} ` ? M : S;
```
options.why: It strips a single space from each end with no recursion, so `A` becomes `' hi '`.

options.text:
```ts
type Trim<S extends string> =
  S extends `${WS}${infer M}${WS}` ? Trim<M> : S;
```
options.why: It only matches when both ends have whitespace, so `B` stays `'hi   '` and `C` stops at `' hi'`.

explanation: String-manipulation types use template literal patterns with `infer` and recursion: match one character class at an edge, strip it, and recurse. Trimming the two ends with separate branches is what makes uneven input work. The interviewer is checking recursion, base cases, and whether you test inputs with whitespace on only one side.

stem:
Which `ReplaceAll` passes every check?

```ts
type A = ReplaceAll<'foboorfoboar', 'bo', 'b'>; // 'foborfobar'
type B = ReplaceAll<'t y p e s', ' ', ''>;     // 'types'
type C = ReplaceAll<'abc', '', 'x'>;            // 'abc'
```

options.text:
```ts
type ReplaceAll<S extends string, F extends string, T extends string> =
  F extends '' ? S
  : S extends `${infer L}${F}${infer R}` ? `${L}${T}${ReplaceAll<R, F, T>}`
  : S;
```
options.why: It guards the empty pattern and recurses only on the text after each match, so replaced output is never scanned again.

options.text:
```ts
type ReplaceAll<S extends string, F extends string, T extends string> =
  F extends '' ? S
  : S extends `${infer L}${F}${infer R}` ? ReplaceAll<`${L}${T}${R}`, F, T>
  : S;
```
options.why: It rescans the string after each replacement, so new matches made by the replacement are replaced too: `A` becomes `'fobrfobar'`.

options.text:
```ts
type ReplaceAll<S extends string, F extends string, T extends string> =
  F extends '' ? S
  : S extends `${infer L}${F}${infer R}` ? `${L}${T}${R}`
  : S;
```
options.why: With no recursion this replaces only the first match: `A` becomes `'foborfoboar'` and `B` becomes `'ty p e s'`.

options.text:
```ts
type ReplaceAll<S extends string, F extends string, T extends string> =
  S extends `${infer L}${F}${infer R}` ? `${L}${T}${ReplaceAll<R, F, T>}`
  : S;
```
options.why: Without the empty-pattern guard, an empty `F` matches after every character, so `C` becomes `'axbxcx'`.

explanation: A correct `ReplaceAll` recurses on the remainder `R`, not on the rebuilt string, and handles the empty pattern explicitly. These two details are the edge cases type-challenge tests check, and they are what an interviewer probes when you say "just recurse".

stem: Which two implementations make `CamelCase<'foo-bar-baz'>` resolve to `'fooBarBaz'`? (Choose two.)

options.text:
```ts
type CamelCase<S extends string> =
  S extends `${infer H}-${infer T}` ? `${H}${CamelCase<Capitalize<T>>}` : S;
```
options.why: It capitalises the rest before recursing, so each segment after a dash starts with a capital letter: `'foo' + 'Bar' + 'Baz'`.

options.text:
```ts
type CamelCase<S extends string> =
  S extends `${infer H}-${infer T}` ? `${H}${Capitalize<CamelCase<T>>}` : S;
```
options.why: It converts the rest first (`'barBaz'`) and then capitalises it (`'BarBaz'`), which gives the same result.

options.text:
```ts
type CamelCase<S extends string> =
  S extends `${infer H}-${infer T}` ? `${Capitalize<H>}${CamelCase<T>}` : S;
```
options.why: It capitalises every segment except the last, giving `'FooBarbaz'`.

options.text:
```ts
type CamelCase<S extends string> =
  S extends `${infer H}-${infer T}` ? `${H}${Capitalize<T>}` : S;
```
options.why: There is no recursion, so only the first dash is handled: `'fooBar-baz'`.

options.text:
```ts
type CamelCase<S extends string> =
  S extends `${infer H}-${infer T}` ? `${H}${Uppercase<CamelCase<T>>}` : S;
```
options.why: `Uppercase` changes every character, not just the first, giving `'fooBARBAZ'`.

explanation: `${infer H}-${infer T}` splits at the first dash, because `H` matches as little as possible. Recurse on the rest and capitalise it, before or after the recursive call. `Capitalize`, `Uncapitalize`, `Uppercase` and `Lowercase` are the built-in intrinsic string types. Interviewers ask for casing conversions to test template literal inference and recursion together.

stem:
Which `Concat` passes both checks exactly?

```ts
const tuple = [1] as const;

type A = Concat<[1], [2, 3]>;        // [1, 2, 3]
type B = Concat<typeof tuple, [2]>; // [1, 2]
```

options.text:
```ts
type Concat<A extends readonly unknown[], B extends readonly unknown[]> =
  [...A, ...B];
```
options.why: The `readonly` constraints accept `as const` tuples, and spreading both into a new tuple type gives a plain mutable tuple with the elements in order.

options.text:
```ts
type Concat<A extends unknown[], B extends unknown[]> =
  [...A, ...B];
```
options.why: `typeof tuple` is `readonly [1]`, which is not assignable to the mutable `unknown[]` constraint, so `B` is a compile error.

options.text:
```ts
type Concat<A extends readonly unknown[], B extends readonly unknown[]> =
  readonly [...A, ...B];
```
options.why: The elements are right, but the result is `readonly [1, 2, 3]`, which a strict equality check treats as a different type from `[1, 2, 3]`.

options.text:
```ts
type Concat<A extends readonly unknown[], B extends readonly unknown[]> =
  [A, ...B];
```
options.why: `A` is not spread, so it becomes a single nested element: `[[1], 2, 3]`.

explanation: Variadic tuple types (TypeScript 4.0) let you spread generic tuple types: `[...A, ...B]`. Constrain the inputs to `readonly unknown[]` so both mutable and `as const` tuples are accepted. Interviewers use `Concat` to check that you know spreads keep positions and that `readonly` is part of a tuple's type.

options.text: `(...tail: [c: boolean]) => number`
options.why: `A` is inferred from the extra arguments as `[number, string]`, and the rest of `add3`'s parameter list, `[c: boolean]`, is left for `B`.

options.text: `(...tail: [b: string, c: boolean]) => number`
options.why: Both leading arguments are captured in `A`, so only the last parameter remains in `B`.

options.text: `(...tail: unknown[]) => number`
options.why: Variadic tuple inference splits the parameter list precisely. It does not fall back to the `unknown[]` constraint.

options.text: The call is a compile error, because TypeScript cannot split a parameter list into two spreads `[...A, ...B]`.
options.why: Splitting a parameter list across generic spreads is the main use case variadic tuples were added for in TypeScript 4.0.

explanation: With variadic tuple types, a generic rest parameter can be split into a known prefix and an inferred remainder. That is how `partial`, `bind` and `curry` get precise types. Calling `f('x')` is an error, and `partial(add3, 'x')` is an error too because `'x'` is not a `number`. The interviewer is checking that you can explain variadic tuples with a real typing problem.

options.why: `U` is added as one element and is never spread, so the tuple `[3]` stays nested. `Unshift` puts `0` at the front.
Only `T` is spread. `U` is placed as a single element even when it is a tuple.

options.text: `A` is a compile error and `B` is `[0, 1, 2]`
options.why: `U` has no constraint, so a tuple is a valid argument for it.
`Unshift` places `U` before the spread `...T`, so `0` comes first.

explanation: A spread `...T` copies a tuple's elements into a new tuple, while a bare type parameter is a single element. `Push` and `Unshift` are warm-up type challenges, and the trick is noticing which side is spread. Interviewers often follow up by asking you to write `Concat`.

stem:
Which `Last` passes both checks?

```ts
type A = Last<[1, 2, 3]>; // 3
type B = Last<[]>;        // never
```

options.why: A leading rest element with `infer` lets the pattern capture the final element, and an empty tuple does not match, which gives `never`.
Prepending one element makes `T['length']` index the last item, so `A` is `3`. But for `[]` it reads `[any][0]`, which is `any`, not `never`.

options.text:
```ts
type Last<T extends unknown[]> =
  T extends [infer L, ...infer _] ? L : never;
```
options.why: This captures the first element, so `A` becomes `1`.
It compiles, but indexes one position past the end, so `A` becomes `undefined`.

explanation: Since TypeScript 4.2, a rest element can appear before other elements, so `[...infer _, infer L]` matches the last element directly. The `[any, ...T][T['length']]` trick is a known answer too, but it gives the wrong result for an empty tuple. Interviewers ask about `Last` to see whether you check edge cases like `[]`.

stem:
Which `Pop` passes both checks?

```ts
type A = Pop<[1, 2, 3]>; // [1, 2]
type B = Pop<[]>;        // []
```

options.text:
```ts
type Pop<T extends unknown[]> =
  T extends [...infer R, unknown] ? R : [];
```
options.why: It captures everything before the last element, and the empty tuple falls through to `[]`.

options.text:
```ts
type Pop<T extends unknown[]> =
  T extends [...infer R, infer _] ? R : never;
```
options.why: The pattern is right, but an empty tuple does not match and falls through to `never`, so `B` fails.

options.text:
```ts
type Pop<T extends unknown[]> =
  T extends [infer _, ...infer R] ? R : [];
```
options.why: This removes the first element (it is `Shift`), so `A` becomes `[2, 3]`.

options.text:
```ts
type Pop<T extends unknown[]> =
  T extends [...infer R] ? R : [];
```
options.why: `[...infer R]` matches the whole tuple, so nothing is removed and `A` stays `[1, 2, 3]`.

explanation: `Pop` is `Last` in reverse: infer the leading rest and ignore the final element. The false branch decides what happens for `[]`, which is what type-challenge tests check. The interviewer wants to see that you think about the fallback branch rather than writing `never` by habit.

stem:
Using the `Equal` helper below, which `Includes` passes all three checks?

```ts
type Equal<X, Y> =
  (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends (<T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2) ? true : false;

type A = Includes<[1, 2, 3], 2>;                         // true
type B = Includes<[boolean], false>;                     // false
type C = Includes<[{ a: 'A' }], { readonly a: 'A' }>;    // false
```

options.text:
```ts
type Includes<T extends readonly unknown[], U> =
  T extends [infer F, ...infer R]
    ? Equal<F, U> extends true ? true : Includes<R, U>
    : false;
```
options.why: It compares each element to `U` with exact type identity, so `boolean` is not `false` and a mutable property is not a `readonly` one.

options.text:
```ts
type Includes<T extends readonly unknown[], U> =
  U extends T[number] ? true : false;
```
options.why: This tests assignability, not identity. `false` is assignable to `boolean`, and the `readonly` object is assignable to the mutable one, so `B` and `C` both become `true`.

options.text:
```ts
type Includes<T extends readonly unknown[], U> =
  T extends [infer F, ...infer R]
    ? F extends U ? true : Includes<R, U>
    : false;
```
options.why: `F extends U` distributes over `boolean`, so `B` becomes `boolean`. And `C` is `true`, because `readonly` does not affect assignability.

options.text:
```ts
type Includes<T extends readonly unknown[], U> =
  T[number] extends U ? true : false;
```
options.why: This asks whether every element is assignable to `U`, so `A` is `false` because `1 | 2 | 3` is not assignable to `2`.

explanation: `Includes` looks trivial until the tests demand exact identity. Assignability (`extends`) treats `false` as a `boolean` and ignores `readonly`, so you need an identity check like the generic-function `Equal` and a recursive walk over the tuple. Interviewers use this to probe the difference between assignability and type equality.

stem:
Which `Paths<T>` makes `Paths<O>` exactly `'id' | 'user' | 'user.name' | 'user.address' | 'user.address.city'`?

```ts
type O = { id: number; user: { name: string; address: { city: string } } };
```

options.text:
```ts
type Paths<T> = T extends object
  ? { [K in keyof T & string]: K | `${K}.${Paths<T[K]>}` }[keyof T & string]
  : never;
```
options.why: Each key contributes itself plus every deeper path prefixed with `key.`. Primitives give `never`, so their prefixed template becomes `never` too, and indexing with `[keyof T & string]` collects everything into one union.

options.text:
```ts
type Paths<T> = T extends object
  ? { [K in keyof T]: K | `${K}.${Paths<T[K]>}` }[keyof T]
  : never;
```
options.why: `keyof T` can include `symbol`, which cannot appear in a template literal type, so this is a compile error.
This only returns leaf paths: `'id' | 'user.name' | 'user.address.city'`. The intermediate `'user'` and `'user.address'` are missing.
Without the final indexed access the result is an object type, not a union, and putting it inside a template literal is a compile error.

explanation: The pattern is: map over the string keys, return each key together with every deeper path prefixed by `key.`, then index the mapped type with its own keys to turn it into a union. `& string` removes symbol and number keys, and a primitive returning `never` ends the recursion. This is the type behind typed form field names and i18n keys, which is why staff-level interviews ask for it.

stem:
A teammate uses this `Paths` to type form field names. Which statement about `Paths<{ tags: string[] }>` is true?

```ts
type Paths<T> = T extends object
  ? { [K in keyof T & string]: K | `${K}.${Paths<T[K]>}` }[keyof T & string]
  : never;
```

options.text: It is just `'tags'`, because `string[]` does not extend `object`.
options.why: Arrays are objects, so they pass the `object` check and their keys are listed.

options.text: It contains `'tags'` and `` `tags.${number}` ``, but no method names.
options.why: `& string` drops the numeric index signature, so no numeric path appears, while the method names are string keys and do appear.

The interviewer wants to see you test the type on realistic data, not only on plain nested objects.

stem: Which `Permutation` gives all six orderings for `Permutation<'A' | 'B' | 'C'>` (such as `['A', 'B', 'C'] | ['A', 'C', 'B'] | ...`) and `[]` for `Permutation<never>`?

```ts
type Permutation<T, K = T> =
  [T] extends [never] ? []
  : K extends K ? [K, ...Permutation<Exclude<T, K>>]
  : never;
```
options.why: `K extends K` distributes over each member, which then goes first, while `T` still holds the full union so `Exclude<T, K>` leaves the rest. `[T] extends [never]` detects the empty union.

options.text:
```ts
type Permutation<T, K = T> =
  T extends never ? []
  : K extends K ? [K, ...Permutation<Exclude<T, K>>]
  : never;
```
options.why: `T extends never` distributes over `never`, which yields `never` instead of `[]`. The base case collapses, so the whole result is `never`.

options.text:
```ts
type Permutation<T> =
  [T] extends [never] ? []
  : T extends T ? [T, ...Permutation<Exclude<T, T>>]
  : never;
```
options.why: Inside the distribution `T` is a single member, so `Exclude<T, T>` is `never` and the result is `['A'] | ['B'] | ['C']`.

options.text:
```ts
type Permutation<T, K = T> =
  [T] extends [never] ? []
  : [K, ...Permutation<Exclude<T, K>>];
```
options.why: Nothing distributes, so `K` is the whole union and the result is `['A' | 'B' | 'C']`.

explanation: `Permutation` combines two tricks: distribute over a copy of the union (`K extends K`) while keeping the full union in another parameter, and detect `never` with the non-distributive check `[T] extends [never]`. It is a staff-level type puzzle that tests whether you really understand distributive conditional types.

options.why: `${infer F}${infer R}` takes one character for `F` and the rest for `R`. The empty string does not match, so it adds `never`, which vanishes from the union.

```ts
type StringToUnion<S extends string> =

```

options.text:
```ts
type StringToUnion<S extends string> =
  S extends `${infer F}${infer R}` ? F : never;
```

explanation: When two `infer` placeholders are adjacent in a template literal, the first one matches exactly one character. That makes character-by-character recursion possible. The detail interviewers watch for is the base case: return `never` so no empty string leaks into the union.

stem: Given `type MyPartial<T> = { [K in keyof T]?: T[K] }`, which two statements are true? (Choose two.)

stem: After implementing `Pick`, you are asked to build `MyOmit` from it. With `interface User { readonly id: number; name: string; email?: string }`, which definition makes `MyOmit<User, 'name'>` equal to `{ readonly id: number; email?: string }`?

options.text: Annotate the exported `createStore`, since it is a public contract and `isolatedDeclarations` requires it, and let `getCartTotals` be inferred, using `ReturnType<typeof getCartTotals>` where needed.
options.why: An explicit type on a public API makes accidental changes fail at the definition. Inference stays the source of truth for private code, and `isolatedDeclarations` reports TS9008 for the unannotated export.

options.text: Infer everything, because `ReturnType<typeof createStore>` always matches the implementation, so annotations add no safety.
options.why: Always matching the implementation is the risk: an accidental change silently becomes the new public type. It also fails under `isolatedDeclarations`.

options.text: Annotate every function, including private helpers, because inferred return types become `any` under `strict`.
options.why: Inferred return types are precise, not `any`. Annotating private helpers is a style choice, not a safety need.

options.text: Avoid `ReturnType` altogether, because it runs the function at compile time and slows the build.
options.why: `ReturnType` is purely a type operation. Nothing is executed.

explanation: Trust inference where the implementation is the source of truth: local helpers, and types derived for internal use with `ReturnType<typeof fn>`. options.text: `{ ok: false; error: string; value?: undefined } | { ok: true; value: number; error?: undefined }`
options.why: When object literals are combined into a union, TypeScript normalises them: each member gets the other members' properties as optional `undefined`, so `result.value` can be read without narrowing.

options.text: `{ ok: false; error: string } | { ok: true; value: number }`
options.why: This is close, but inferred unions of object literals are normalised with the missing properties added as optional `undefined`.

options.text: `{ ok: boolean; error: string; value: number }`
options.why: The two returns are not merged into one object. `as const` keeps `ok` as the literals `false` and `true`, and the union is kept.

options.text: `{ ok: boolean; error?: string; value?: number }`

Without `as const`, `ok` would widen to `boolean` and the discriminant would be lost. Interviewers ask this to check that you inspect inferred types rather than guessing.

stem: Given `interface User { id: number; name: string; email: string }`, which two definitions of `PartialBy<T, K>` accept `{ name: 'x' }` as a `PartialBy<User, 'id' | 'email'>` while still rejecting `{}`? (Choose two.)

options.why: `Omit<T, 'id'>` keeps `name` and `email`. `Exclude` works on unions, not object keys, so the change would break the type.

stem: The reverse utility, `RequiredBy`, should make chosen keys required. Given `interface Opt { id?: number; name?: string; age: number }`, which two definitions reject `{ age: 2 }` as a `RequiredBy<Opt, 'id'>` while keeping `name` optional? (Choose two.)

`Pick` copies `?` from `Opt`, so `id` stays optional and `{ age: 2 }` is accepted.
This is the wrong way round: `name` becomes required and `id` stays optional.

stem: Given `interface Todo { title: string; description?: string; completed: boolean }`, which `MyReadonly2` makes only `title` read-only in `MyReadonly2<Todo, 'title'>`, keeps `description` optional, and makes every key read-only when you write `MyReadonly2<Todo>`?

```ts
type MyReadonly2<T, K extends keyof T = keyof T> =
  Readonly<Pick<T, K>> & Omit<T, K>;
```
options.why: The chosen keys become read-only, the rest keep their modifiers through `Omit`, and the default `keyof T` covers the one-argument form.

```ts
type MyReadonly2<T, K extends keyof T> =

```

```ts
type MyReadonly2<T, K extends keyof T = keyof T> =

```
